subsystems.name: Tissue preservation and sectioning
subsystems.role: turns a whole brain into a stable, sliceable block whose wiring survives the process.

subsystems.name: Volume electron microscopy
subsystems.role: images every section at a resolution fine enough to see synapses — a few nanometres per pixel.

subsystems.name: Image alignment and segmentation
subsystems.role: stitches millions of images into one volume and traces each neuron and synapse out of the pixel data.

subsystems.name: Connectome graph and annotation
subsystems.role: stores the result as a graph of neurons and their connections, labelled by cell type and synapse type.

subsystems.name: Functional mapping
subsystems.role: captures what the circuit actually does, not just how it is wired.

subsystems.name: Emulation substrate
subsystems.role: runs the reconstructed network as a simulation.

buildSteps.title: Fix and stain the brain
buildSteps.detail: The tissue is chemically fixed so structure stops changing, then soaked in heavy-metal stains that make membranes and synapses visible to electrons.

buildSteps.title: Embed and slice
buildSteps.detail: The brain is set in resin and cut into tens of thousands of ultrathin sections, each a few tens of nanometres thick, collected in order on tape or wafers.

buildSteps.title: Image every section
buildSteps.detail: A multi-beam electron microscope scans each section, producing a stack of images that, for a human brain, would total on the order of exabytes — far beyond any dataset built so far.

buildSteps.title: Align the stack
buildSteps.detail: Software registers each image to its neighbours so that a single dendrite can be followed across thousands of sections without drifting apart.

buildSteps.title: Trace neurons and find synapses
buildSteps.detail: Machine-learning models segment cell membranes and flag the tiny junctions where one neuron contacts another; human proofreaders correct the errors, which is currently the slowest and most expensive step.

buildSteps.title: Type the cells and synapses
buildSteps.detail: Structure alone does not say whether a synapse is excitatory or inhibitory, or which receptor it uses. Extra molecular labelling — or paired recordings and gene-expression data — is needed to give each node and edge a functional meaning.

buildSteps.title: Add activity
buildSteps.detail: Recordings from the same or a comparable brain are used to fit a model that reproduces its firing patterns, since a wiring diagram at one instant says little about dynamics, glia, neuromodulators or plasticity.

buildSteps.title: Run the emulation
buildSteps.detail: The annotated graph is loaded onto a computer that integrates each neuron's state over time. Doing this for a human brain, at speeds that keep pace with real life, is many orders of magnitude beyond current machines.

buildSteps.title: Validate — and confront the open question
buildSteps.detail: The emulation's behaviour would be compared against the original. Whether a sufficiently accurate simulation would itself be conscious is not a question any current method can test; a copy is also not the same as transferring a mind.

prerequisites.why: complete maps exist for a nematode and, since 2024, the adult fruit fly; a whole mouse brain and certainly a human brain remain out of reach.
machine learning does most of the tracing, but the remaining human correction is a decades-scale bottleneck at human volumes.
micrographs show a junction but not its transmitter, receptor type or strength — essential for a functional, not just structural, copy.

prerequisites.tech: Non-destructive scanning of a living brain
prerequisites.why: every technique described here kills and slices the tissue; no known method reads a living human connectome intact, which is the core requirement for 'uploading' a person rather than reconstructing a deceased one.
exascale machines exist, but real-time simulation of ~10^14 synapses with biologically detailed models would need a further leap of many orders of magnitude.
without one, there is no way to tell whether an emulation experiences anything, so the central promise cannot be verified.

pathway.milestone: complete connectomes of small organisms and of small mammalian volumes, paired with activity data
pathway.unlocks: proof that dense reconstruction and functional mapping can be joined at all.

pathway.milestone: a complete mouse brain connectome with cell types and recorded activity
pathway.unlocks: the first mammal-scale emulation, useful for neuroscience and as a crude benchmark.

pathway.milestone: molecular-resolution synapse typing and proofreading automated to near-zero human effort
pathway.unlocks: human-scale reconstruction becomes an engineering cost rather than a lifetime project.

pathway.milestone: a post-mortem human connectome, reconstructed as a non-conscious model of that individual's circuits
pathway.unlocks: research uses and a hard test of whether structure alone reproduces behaviour.

pathway.milestone: a non-destructive, living-brain readout — currently no known physical mechanism
pathway.unlocks: the only route by which 'uploading' would mean anything other than making a digital copy of a dead brain.
